key_concept: An ideal Zener diode in reverse breakdown holds a fixed voltage $|V_Z|$ across itself, and the series resistor drops the rest: $V_R = |V_i| - |V_Z|$.
steps: The circuit is a single series loop: battery → Zener diode (C–B) → resistor R (B–A) → back to the battery. The same current flows through every element.
The diode is reverse biased with $|V_i| = 5\ \text{V}$, which exceeds the breakdown magnitude $|V_Z| = 3\ \text{V}$. So the Zener is in breakdown.
An ideal Zener in breakdown keeps a constant voltage across itself: $|V_{CB}| = 3\ \text{V}$.
Apply KVL around the loop: $|V_i| = |V_Z| + |V_R|$, so $|V_R| = 5 - 3 = 2\ \text{V}$.
Points B and A are the two ends of the resistor. Hence $|V_B - V_A| = 2\ \text{V}$.
why_not_others: 3 V is the voltage across the Zener (C to B), not across the resistor (B to A). 0 V would be correct only if the Zener were not conducting, but $5\ \text{V} > 3\ \text{V}$, so breakdown occurs and current flows.
common_trap: Students often take the voltage between B and A as the Zener voltage (3 V) without checking which element actually lies between those two points.
time_saving_tip: Check $|V_i| > |V_Z|$. If true, the resistor voltage is simply $|V_i| - |V_Z|$.
